title: Designing Modules and Application Boundaries
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of designing modules and application boundaries in a Ruby program and name the key rule involved.
Apply designing modules and application boundaries in a small example and predict its result before running it.
Identify one boundary or failure case related to avoiding circular dependencies and verify the intended behavior.

content.intro: Learn Designing Modules and Application Boundaries through a visual model, a minimal Ruby example, and a practical check.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding designing modules and application boundaries helps you write code that is easier to explain, test, and maintain. It also helps separate Ruby language guarantees from runtime assumptions, dependency behavior, and application-specific rules.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Designing Modules and Application Boundaries helps you reason about separating responsibilities. In Ruby, prefer a small example whose inputs and expected result are easy to explain. This lesson connects the syllabus topic to practical code and highlights where assumptions or edge cases matter.

content_blocks.title: How to think about it
content_blocks.text: Begin by identifying the key rule: Separating responsibilities. Then connect it to Namespacing internal implementation. The remaining syllabus points—Avoiding circular dependencies—are useful checks before applying this in a larger project.

content_blocks.title: Example: Designing Modules and Application Boundaries
content_blocks.code:
module Timestamped
  def timestamp_label
    "created at: #{Time.now.year}"
  end
end
class Report
  include Timestamped
end
puts Report.new.timestamp_label

items.title: Assuming the happy path is enough
items.text: Test an empty value, a boundary value, and one invalid value before depending on the behavior.

items.title: Treating an example as a universal rule
items.text: Check Ruby version, runtime implementation, and third-party library documentation when behavior is version-sensitive.

items.title: Mixing too many concerns
items.text: Separate input parsing, domain behavior, and output so each piece is easier to test.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Run the example as written, compare it with the expected result, and explain why each line supports designing modules and application boundaries. Next change one input or condition and predict the result before running it.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a second example for designing modules and application boundaries using a different input. Add one edge case from the syllabus list (Avoiding circular dependencies), state the expected behavior, and write a small test or manual check that would catch a regression.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain designing modules and application boundaries, identify its place in modules, mixins, and code organization, run a focused example, and verify an important boundary. Revisit the linked exercise if this is a core topic; advanced runtime or framework examples remain draft until reviewed in a suitable environment.
